stops.name: Babylon: Cyrus enters in peace, the Cylinder proclaimed
stops.campa: On the third of Arahsamnu, Cyrus himself enters Babylon. Green branches are spread before him; there is no plunder, no burning. He takes the hand of Bel-Marduk in the New Year rite and is proclaimed king of the four quarters. On a clay barrel his scribes write his charter to the world: Marduk sought a righteous king and chose Cyrus of Anshan; he entered Babylon as a friend; he freed the peoples of their bondage and sent the captured gods and displaced nations home to their own places. The Jews in exile hear that their turn has come.
stops.quote: I am Cyrus, king of the world, great king, mighty king, king of Babylon, king of Sumer and Akkad, king of the four quarters... When I went as harbinger of peace into Babylon I founded my sovereign residence within the palace amid celebration and rejoicing.

stops.name: Babylon, the gods and the peoples sent home
stops.campa: The first act of the new king is to undo the gathering of captives that the kings of Babylon had made. The statues of the gods that Nabonidus dragged into the city, from Ashur and Susa, from Akkad, Eshnunna, Zamban, Der, all the shrines across the Tigris, Cyrus sends back unharmed to their own sanctuaries, and rebuilds the ruined temples. And with the gods he sends the peoples: he gathers all the displaced nations that Babylon had uprooted and returns them, each to its own settlement. Into this great homing of captives the exiles of Judah are folded, and their turn comes with the rest.
stops.quote: I returned the images of the gods, who had resided there, to their places and I let them dwell in eternal abodes. I gathered all their inhabitants and returned to them their dwellings.

stops.name: Babylon, the edict of return proclaimed
stops.campa: In the first year of his reign over Babylon, the Lord stirs the spirit of Cyrus, and he sends a proclamation through all his kingdom, and writes it also: the God of heaven has given him all the kingdoms of the earth and charged him to build a house at Jerusalem. Let the people of that God go up; let their neighbours help them with silver and gold and beasts and freewill offerings for the house. So the word goes out that is the exact answer to seventy years of weeping by the rivers of Babylon.
stops.quote: Thus saith Cyrus king of Persia, The LORD God of heaven hath given me all the kingdoms of the earth; and he hath charged me to build him an house at Jerusalem, which is in Judah. Who is there among you of all his people? ... let him go up.

stops.name: Babylon, the vessels of the Temple restored
stops.campa: Cyrus commands the treasurer Mithredath to bring out the vessels of the house of the Lord that Nebuchadnezzar carried off from Jerusalem and set in the house of his gods: the very gold cups Belshazzar profaned at his last feast. They are counted out to Sheshbazzar, prince of Judah: chargers of gold and silver, basins, knives, bowls, five thousand four hundred vessels in all. The plunder of the fallen Temple is handed back for the Temple to come. What the moon-drunk kings of Babylon took, the anointed of the east returns.
stops.quote: Cyrus the king brought forth the vessels of the house of the LORD, which Nebuchadnezzar had brought forth out of Jerusalem, and had put them in the house of his gods.

stops.name: Jerusalem, the foundations of the Second Temple laid
stops.campa: The exiles go up, some fifty thousand, with Zerubbabel and Jeshua the priest, on the long road from Babylon to the ruined city. In the seventh month they set the altar on its old base and offer the burnt sacrifice; in the second year they lay the Temple's foundation. The priests sound trumpets, the Levites clash cymbals and sing that the Lord is good; the young shout for joy, while the old men who saw the first house weep aloud, so that weeping and shouting cannot be told apart. Isaiah's word is fulfilled: Cyrus is the Lord's shepherd, his anointed, who says of the Temple, let it be built.
stops.quote: Thus saith the LORD to his anointed, to Cyrus, whose right hand I have holden, to subdue nations before him... even saying to Jerusalem, Thou shalt be built; and to the temple, Thy foundation shall be laid.

stops.name: Susa: the older Elamite throne, the roads made one
stops.campa: Cyrus takes into his empire the ancient Elamite seat of Susa on the lowland rivers, joining it to Anshan as of old, so that the twin heartland of Elam is whole again under one king. From Susa the royal road will one day run to Sardis. He has bound the plateau and the two great river-lands and the sea-coast into a single realm larger than any before it, and he has ruled it not by terror but, the nations say, by giving each people its own gods and its own law. He is called father.

stops.name: The Araxes frontier, the marriage refused
stops.campa: Beyond the last river, on the open steppe, rule the Massagetae: horse-nomads who drink no wine, know no farming, and worship only the sun, to whom they sacrifice the swiftest of horses. Their queen is Tomyris, a widow. Cyrus, master of half the world, sends to ask her hand: meaning not the woman but the kingdom. She sees through it and refuses. So Cyrus prepares to take by the sword what he could not take by the ring, and begins to bridge the Araxes to carry his army across into her land.
stops.quote: King of the Medes, cease to press this matter... Rule your own people, and endure to see me ruling mine.

stops.name: Across the Araxes, the banquet-trap and the capture of Spargapises
stops.campa: Tomyris offers to withdraw three days' march and let Cyrus cross to fight on her ground, or to do the same herself. On Croesus's counsel Cyrus crosses and lays a trap: he leaves his camp with a feast spread and much wine, and the weakest of his troops in it, then withdraws. A third of the Massagetae fall on the camp, kill the guards, and, knowing nothing of wine, gorge and grow drunk. The Persians return and slaughter or take them sleeping. Among the captured is Spargapises, the queen's son and the army's commander.

stops.name: The steppe, the death of Spargapises and the oath of Tomyris
stops.campa: Spargapises wakes from the wine to find himself a prisoner. He begs to be unbound, and the moment his hands are free he kills himself, unable to bear the shame. Tomyris, hearing that her son is dead and her army tricked with the drug the Persians call wine, sends Cyrus a herald with a terrible oath: sun-glutton, do not boast; give me back my son and go, or I swear by the Sun, lord of the Massagetae, I will give you your fill of blood.
stops.quote: Give me back my son and leave my country unharmed... If you will not, I swear by the sun, the lord of the Massagetae, that I will give you your fill of blood, insatiable as you are.

stops.name: The last battle: Cyrus falls, and the head in the wineskin
stops.campa: The two hosts join in the fiercest battle Herodotus knows of between barbarians. They stand and shoot until the arrows are spent, then close with spear and dagger and grapple hand to hand for a long time, neither yielding. At last the Massagetae prevail; the great part of the Persian army is destroyed, and Cyrus himself is killed, after twenty-nine years of reign. Tomyris seeks his body among the dead, fills a skin with human blood, and thrusts his severed head into it, making good her oath: glut yourself on blood, of which you could never have enough.
stops.quote: Though I live and conquer you, you have destroyed me still, for you took my son by guile; but I will make good my threat, and give you your fill of blood.
stops.quote_source: Tomyris over the head of Cyrus, Herodotus, Histories 1.214

stops.name: Pasargadae: the tomb, and the plea to the passer-by
stops.campa: His body is brought home, the traditions say, to Pasargadae, the city he raised on the field where he first became king. There he is laid in the plain stone house on its six great steps: no vast pyramid, no boast in bronze, only a small chamber holding a golden bed and coffin and the king's ornaments, guarded by the Magi. Upon it, the Greeks record, stands the inscription that speaks to every man who will ever pass: I am Cyrus, who won the empire for the Persians; do not grudge me this little earth that covers my body. Two centuries on, Alexander stands here, reads it, and weeps.
stops.quote: O man, whoever you are and wherever you come from, for I know you will come — I am Cyrus, who won for the Persians their empire. Do not therefore begrudge me this little earth that covers my body.
stops.quote_source: The tomb-inscription of Cyrus, as recorded by Aristobulus in Strabo, Geography 15.3.7; cf. Plutarch, Life of Alexander 69
